title: Compliance Run
subtitle: A beginner's escape through a haunted bakehouse, about following the rules at work and why they matter

paragraphs: Pip just started work at Sunny Bakes, a small chain of bakeries. In one week the food inspector visits. Pip has heard the word **compliance** a dozen times already and still isn't sure what it means.

Tonight Pip dreams of the old, haunted bakehouse. The ghosts of every check anybody ever skipped are on Pip's heels. Seven stretches of the escape each teach one thing about compliance, and at the end of each a guardian of the bakehouse asks about it.
steps: Read the short lesson, then press **Run**. Arrows or swipes change lane, **up** jumps, **down** slides; at a corner, press the way the path turns.
Some guardians ask in a card. Others set a trial on the track: collect the glowing votes, run through the right lane, jump the false planks.
A wrong answer shows you why and the ghosts drift a little closer. You always get through; first-try answers earn three stars.
intro.note: Sunny Bakes, Pip and every number in this game are made up to teach the idea. The ideas apply to any organisation, from a bakery to a bank.

stretches.name: Rulebook Run
stretches.lead: Everyone at Sunny Bakes keeps saying "compliance". Pip asked seven coworkers what it means and got a mix of answers. The honest answer is simple: compliance means **following the rules that apply to you**. The laws of the country, the regulations for your industry, the standards you've signed up to, and your own organisation's policies.
body: The coworkers' answers were: **A** following the rules that apply to us, **B** paperwork that nobody reads, **C** something only lawyers do, **D** saying yes to the boss.

activity.prompt: The seven answers float over the path ahead as glowing letters. Run through all seven to collect them. Each one is a vote.
activity.resultNote: Three coworkers had other ideas. That's normal: the word sounds grander than it is.

quiz.question: In plain words, what is compliance?

options.text: Following the rules that apply to your organisation
Paperwork that nobody reads
options.why: Paperwork is sometimes how you prove you followed a rule, but it isn't the point. The rule is the point.

options.text: Something only lawyers do
options.why: Lawyers help explain the rules, but it's the people doing the work, like Pip, who follow them every day.

stretches.remember: Compliance means following the rules that apply to you: laws, regulations, standards and your own policies.

stretches.name: Rule-Makers Hall
stretches.lead: Where do the rules come from? Not from one place. Four kinds of rule-maker stand in this hall. The taller the figure, the more people its rules reach.
body: **Laws** are made by parliaments and governments and apply to everyone in the country. **Regulations** are detailed rules from a regulator, such as a food safety agency, for one industry. **Standards** are agreed good practice that organisations sign up to, often to earn a certificate. **Policies** are the rules an organisation writes for itself, like Sunny Bakes' rule "check every fridge twice a day".

activity.prompt: Pip's manager says: "Our own rule is that every fridge is checked twice a day." Which kind of rule is that? Pick its pad.

options.label: Law
options.hint: Laws come from the government and apply to everyone. A rule the bakery wrote for itself is something smaller.

options.label: Regulation
options.hint: A regulator might say "keep food cold". "Check twice a day" is how Sunny Bakes chose to do that: a rule of its own.

options.label: Standard
options.hint: Standards are shared good practice that many organisations sign up to. This rule belongs to Sunny Bakes alone.

aside.title: Why so many layers?
aside.text: The outer rules say **what** must be true: food must be safe. The inner ones say **how** your organisation makes sure of it: check the fridge twice a day. Policies are how a big, vague law becomes a small, doable habit.

stretches.remember: Laws, regulations and standards come from outside. Policies are the rules your organisation writes for itself to meet them.

stretches.name: Training Tunnel
stretches.lead: A policy that nobody knows about protects nobody. So organisations **train** people when they start and remind them along the way. Pip's first week has a food-safety course, a short quiz, and a poster by every fridge.

activity.title: Try it: spread the fridge rule

readout.text: No training, no reminders. The policy is a document in a drawer. Roughly {30 + t + r*2} of 100 staff would remember the fridge rule, and only by luck.
Rough idea: about {30 + t + r*2} of 100 staff remember the fridge rule on a busy Saturday.

cases.text: Nearly everyone knows the rule and why it exists. This is what good training looks like: regular, short, and backed up by reminders where the work happens.
Good training, but on a busy Saturday people forget. Put a reminder where the work happens: right by the fridge.
Posters help people remember, but nobody has been taught what the numbers on the thermometer mean. Add some training.

fallback.text: Most of the team can't say what the fridge rule is. The policy exists only on paper. Try more training and a reminder or two.

activity.caption: The numbers are made up to show one idea: knowing a rule takes both teaching and reminding. The squares are the staff who remember the rule; the grey slabs are the posters.

quiz.question: Sunny Bakes writes a great fridge policy and files it in the office. Is the job done?

options.text: Yes, the rule exists now
options.why: A rule nobody knows about protects nobody. Try the sliders above with zero training.

options.text: No, people need to be trained and reminded

stretches.remember: Policies only work when people know them. Training and reminders turn a document into a habit.

stretches.name: Check-Up Cliffs
stretches.lead: How does anyone know the rules are really being followed? Two ways. **Monitoring** is the everyday checking you do yourself: the fridge log, the weekly walk-round. An **audit** is when someone from outside the team, or outside the organisation, comes to check the checks.
body: Three Sunny Bakes shops. Last spring the inspector found **30** problems at Oak Street, **42** at Harbour and **18** at Hilltop. This autumn, after every shop started a weekly self-check, the inspector found **24**, **9** and **15**. The numbers are made up to show the pattern.

findings.caption: Problems found by the inspector (made-up numbers). Grey: last spring. Colour: this autumn, after weekly self-checks began.
findings.text: Harbour went from 42 problems to 9, the biggest drop by far. Its manager did the self-check every Monday and fixed what it found the same day. Monitoring catches slips early; the audit then confirms that the monitoring works.

activity.prompt: Three rune stones float over the lanes, one per shop. Run through the shop that improved the most.

options.label: Oak Street
options.hint: Oak Street improved a little, from 30 to 24. One shop improved far more.

options.label: Hilltop
options.hint: Hilltop only moved from 18 to 15. Look for the biggest drop.

stretches.remember: Monitoring is checking your own work every day. An audit is someone else checking that your checks work.

stretches.name: Slip-Up Stairs
stretches.lead: What actually happens when a rule is broken? Pip imagines a quiet Tuesday at the Harbour shop, back before the self-checks started.

frames: Tuesday morning. The fridge is making a strange noise, but it's busy, and nobody writes the temperature in the log.
By Thursday the cream has been too warm for two days. It smells fine. Nobody notices.
Friday. Six customers who ate the cream cakes fall ill. One of them is a child.
The food safety regulator investigates. The log has gaps. The shop closes for a week, pays a fine, and the story is in the local paper.
Now rewind. On a different Tuesday, a baker notices the noise, logs it, tells the manager, and the cream is thrown out. Cost: one tub of cream and five minutes.
activity.caption: A made-up story. Real incidents follow the same shape: a small skipped step, then a big consequence.

aside.title: When something does go wrong
aside.text: Good organisations don't hide it. They **report** it, fix the harm, tell the regulator if the rules say so, and change the process so it can't happen the same way again. Many places protect people who speak up, so fear of blame doesn't keep a slip secret.

quiz.question: Pip notices the fridge is making a strange noise on a busy day. What's the right move?

options.text: Keep serving; it's probably nothing
options.why: That's exactly how the story began. A noisy fridge is a small sign worth two minutes.

options.text: Log it and tell the manager straight away
Quietly fix it later and tell no one
options.why: Fixing is good, but hiding it means nobody can check the food, learn from it, or spot a pattern.

stretches.remember: Breaking a rule rarely hurts only the rule-breaker. Spot it, report it, fix it, learn from it.

stretches.name: Cost Clock
stretches.lead: People often see compliance as a cost: time spent on logs and training instead of baking. So let's actually compare the time.

findings.caption: Hours in a year (illustrative)

rows.label: Fridge checks for a whole year

findings.text: The daily checks for a whole year add up to about 30 hours. A single incident can swallow hundreds of hours, plus the fine and the lost trust. That's why organisations think of compliance as **insurance**, not red tape.

bars.label: Checking the fridge and writing it down

activity.caption: Rough, made-up figures. A twice-daily check takes a few minutes. One incident means closure, investigation, lost customers and sleepless nights.

quiz.question: Over a year, which costs Sunny Bakes more time?

options.text: Doing all the daily checks
options.why: They add up to about 30 hours a year. Press the button above and watch the other bar.

options.text: One serious incident

stretches.remember: Prevention costs minutes. Cleaning up costs weeks. Compliance is insurance.

stretches.name: Culture Bridge
stretches.lead: Last island. Two bakeries can have the same rulebook and be completely different places. In one, people tick the box and look away. In the other, people follow the rule because they understand who it protects, and they speak up when something looks wrong.
body: This is what people mean by **compliance culture**. It shows in small things: whether the manager thanks the baker who throws out the cream, whether questions are welcome, whether the log is filled in honestly when nobody is watching.
Rules set the floor. Culture decides whether people actually stand on it.

findings.caption: Staff who say they would report a problem (illustrative survey, out of 100)
findings.text: Made-up numbers, real pattern: where speaking up is welcomed, problems surface and get fixed. Where it's punished, problems go quiet, and quiet problems grow.

stretches.remember: Box-ticking follows the letter of the rule. Culture follows its purpose. Aim for the second.

activity.prompt: The rope bridge's glowing planks each carry a statement about compliance culture. Step on the true ones. Jump over the false ones.

planks.text: Perfect paperwork proves a culture is strong
planks.why: Paperwork that hides problems is box-ticking; culture is what people actually do.

planks.text: People speak up more where reporters are thanked
Silence usually means there are no problems
planks.why: Silence usually means problems are hidden, not absent.

planks.text: Culture is what people do when nobody watches

finale.name: Inspection Day sprint
finale.lead: The ghosts are right behind you and the sun is coming up. Help Pip handle each situation the way a well-run bakery would, while you run for the door.

questions.question: A new rule from the food safety regulator arrives. What should Sunny Bakes do first?

options.text: Ignore it until the inspector mentions it
options.why: Regulations apply whether or not anyone has checked yet.

options.text: Turn it into a clear policy and train everyone on it
Ask the lawyers to argue it doesn't apply
options.why: Sometimes a rule genuinely doesn't apply, but the normal job is to understand it and build it into daily work.

questions.okText: Correct! Outside rules become inside policies, and policies become habits through training.

questions.question: The weekly self-check finds the freezer at Oak Street is too warm. Nobody got ill. Is it worth writing down?

options.text: No, nothing happened
options.why: Nothing happened **because** the check caught it. Writing it down shows the monitoring works and helps spot a pattern.

options.text: Yes, record it and fix it

questions.okText: Correct! A near miss written down is a lesson learned.

questions.question: Pip's manager says: "Just sign the log for yesterday, nobody will know." What should Pip do?

options.text: Sign it; it's only a form
options.why: A false record is worse than a gap. It hides the truth from the people the rule protects.

options.text: Leave the gap and tell the manager why
Sign it but feel bad about it
options.why: Feeling bad doesn't make the record true.

questions.okText: Correct! An honest gap can be fixed. A false record can't.

questions.question: Which of these best describes a bakery with a strong compliance culture?

options.text: Nobody ever reports a problem
options.why: Silence usually means problems are hidden, not absent.

options.text: Problems get reported, fixed and talked about
The rulebook is the longest in town
options.why: Length isn't the point. Knowing and following the rules is.

questions.okText: Correct! Culture is what people do when the inspector isn't there.

report.heading: Pip made it out!

tiers.perfect: Every answer right first time. The ghosts of missed checks never stood a chance.
tiers.great: Almost perfect. Pip is ready for the inspector.
tiers.pass: You got Pip out of the bakehouse! Run it again to earn more stars.

lessons: Compliance means following the rules that apply to you: laws, regulations, standards and your own policies.
Laws, regulations and standards come from outside; policies are the rules your organisation writes for itself.
Policies only work when people know them: train and remind.
Monitoring is checking your own work; an audit checks the checks.
When a rule is broken, spot it, report it, fix it and learn from it.
Prevention costs minutes; cleaning up costs weeks.
Box-ticking follows the letter of the rule; culture follows its purpose.
report.glossaryIntro: When you hear these words at work, this is what they mean:

glossary.term: The rules that apply to you
Rules the bakery writes for itself
The fridge course and the posters
Telling the manager about the noisy fridge
glossary.meaning: Incident reporting; whistleblowing when it is serious

glossary.term: Doing it right when nobody's watching
